t: "God the Father" or "the God and Father"?
p: Some editions and the KJV read 'God and the Father of our Lord'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort
Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'God and the Father')

why: The editions differ. 'God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ' is Paul's usual phrase (Romans 15:6; 2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3), so a copyist could have added 'and' to match it; the Plain English Translation follows the shorter text of SBLGNT and NA28. The meaning is nearly the same.
b: The editions are as the STEPBible word list marks them.

t: Epaphras serves "for our sake" or "for your sake"?
p: One letter in Greek: ἡμῶν 'our' or ὑμῶν 'your'. The Plain English Translation follows SBLGNT and THGNT; NA28 reads 'your'.

readings.w: P46 (about 200), Sinaiticus (01) first hand, A (02), B (03), D (06) first hand, F, G, 326 first hand, 1505; SBLGNT, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

Sinaiticus corrector, C (04), D corrector, Ψ, 075, 33, 1175, 1739, 1881, 2464, the Byzantine majority, Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions; NA28, NA27, the Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'for you')

why: The Plain English Translation follows SBLGNT and the Tyndale House edition against NA28. The NET Bible's note weighs both sides. 'Our' could have come from a copyist's slip (the same word stands seventeen letters earlier) or from matching the 'we' around it. 'Your' is, in the NET's words, 'somewhat harder', and it too could have come from a slip after the preceding hyper. Since the internal evidence 'can be variously interpreted', the NET decides on the manuscripts, which strongly support 'our'. On that reading Epaphras serves Christ as Paul's representative among them; on the other he serves Christ for the Colossians' good.
b: Witness lists from the NET Bible's note on this verse; editions from the STEPBible word list.

t: "What he has seen" or "what he has not seen"?
p: The KJV's 'things which he hath not seen' follows a later reading that adds 'not'.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01) first hand, A (02), B (03), D first hand, Old Latin d and e, Coptic, Ethiopic; Tertullian and Origen; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT

readings.plain: the things he has not seen

why: The oldest witnesses lack 'not'. With it, the visionary claims what he never saw, which is easier sense; that is why copyists probably added it. F and G read 'not' with a different Greek word (οὐκ), a sign of separate attempts to fix a hard phrase.
b: Witness lists from J. B. Lightfoot's note on the readings (1875), who judged the negative 'a later correction'. Lightfoot even suspected an early copying error behind all the manuscripts (see the note).

a: Nympha, and the church that meets in her house
t: Nympha or Nymphas: "her house," "his house" or "their house"?
p: A woman's name with 'her', or a man's with 'his'? The manuscripts give all three pronouns.

readings.w: B (03), 0278, 6, 1739 first hand, 1881, Sahidic; SBLGNT, NA28, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: Νύμφαν καὶ τὴν κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῆς ἐκκλησίαν

readings.plain: Nympha, and the church that meets in her house

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), A (02), C (04), P, 075, 33, 81, 104, 326, 1175, 2464, Bohairic; Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles
readings.plain: Nympha, and the church that meets in their house

why: 'Her' is the harder reading: copyists were more likely to turn a woman who hosted a church into a man than the reverse. 'Their' may come from uncertainty about the name, or from including the brothers of Laodicea. The Tyndale House edition, which the Plain English Translation often follows, prints 'their' here; the Plain English Translation follows SBLGNT and NA28.
b: The name's gender in Greek depends on an accent (Νύμφαν or Νυμφᾶν), and the oldest manuscripts have no accents, so the pronoun decides. Lightfoot (1875) discussed both forms. Witness lists from the NET Bible note.

p: The Byzantine text adds 'Amen'; the Textus Receptus adds a note on where the letter was written.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'Amen')

why: 'Amen' was often added at the end of letters read in worship. The critical editions leave it out.
b: The Textus Receptus also prints a closing note, 'Written from Rome to the Colossians by Tychicus and Onesimus', printed in the KJV after the verse. Such subscriptions were added by later copyists and are not part of the letter; this one gives the traditional view that Paul wrote from Rome.
